questions.question:
D4 — Reduce scope to the classes the plan actually motivates, or proceed with all 4 new classes across 12 files?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, Step 0 complexity gate.
ELI10: The plan adds four new classes but only explains two of them. AuthBroker and SessionMint are the new services, and AuthCache is a thin wrapper over a cache adapter you already have. TokenStore and RequestPolicy appear only in the file-count line (PLAN.md:35) with no job described. Every unexplained class is surface area that has to be tested, reviewed, and kept in sync with the existing adapter. The question is whether to build all four now or land the two motivated ones plus the facade and add the rest when a concrete need shows up.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Overbuild and you carry two classes nobody can explain in code review, with a real chance TokenStore duplicates the adapter's tenant-keyed storage. Underbuild and you come back for a second PR if TokenStore or RequestPolicy turn out to be load-bearing.
Recommendation: A because the plan text gives TokenStore and RequestPolicy zero responsibilities, and the existing adapter already owns token storage and invalidation. Fewer moving parts, same stated goal, and the eng preference for engineered-enough over premature abstraction.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=10/10, C=6/10
Net: three classes you can defend in review versus four where two are speculative.

options.label: A) Reduce: 3 classes, ~8 files (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Keeps AuthBroker, SessionMint, and the AuthCache facade; defers TokenStore and RequestPolicy until the plan states what they do (human: ~3 days / CC: ~1 hr)
✅ Removes the likely overlap between TokenStore and the existing tenant-keyed adapter before it is written
❌ If RequestPolicy is secretly required for multi-tenant routing, it lands in a follow-up PR instead of this one

options.label: B) Proceed as-is: 4 classes, 12 files
options.description:
✅ Nothing deferred; whatever TokenStore and RequestPolicy were meant to do ships in one PR (human: ~5 days / CC: ~2 hr)
✅ Single review cycle instead of two if the extra classes really are needed
❌ Two classes with no written responsibility, so reviewers and tests have nothing to check them against

options.label: C) Reduce further: drop AuthCache facade too
options.description:
✅ Smallest possible diff; both services call the existing adapter directly (human: ~2 days / CC: ~45 min)
✅ No new cache surface, so no facade drift from the adapter it wraps
❌ Both services must re-implement whatever service-facing shaping the facade was going to centralize, a DRY hit

questions.question:
D5 — Issue 1 [P1] (confidence 8/10) PLAN.md:19-20 — AuthBroker and SessionMint share a module-level mutable AuthCache and both write to it. How should the shared cache be wired?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, Section 1 Architecture.
ELI10: Right now the plan exports one cache object from a module and has two services reach for it and change it. That means nobody owns it: test files stomp on each other's cache state, two writers can interleave on the same tenant key with no coordination (PLAN.md:10 says the adapter does not serialize mutations), and a future third caller can mutate it from anywhere without a reviewer noticing. Passing the cache into each service's constructor from one composition point keeps a single instance in production while making every dependency visible and every test isolated.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Keep the global and a SessionMint write racing an AuthBroker revocation can leave a revoked token cached for a suspended tenant, a cross-tenant security incident that no unit test can reproduce because the tests share the same global.
Recommendation: A because it is Layer 1 practice for Node.js services, costs a constructor parameter per service, and satisfies explicit-over-clever. It also makes the write-ownership rule enforceable in code.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=3/10
Net: one composition root and two constructor parameters versus an invisible global that every test and every future caller can corrupt.

options.label: 1A) Inject + single writer (recommended)
options.description:
✅ AuthCache passed by constructor from one composition root; AuthBroker is the only writer, SessionMint reads and requests invalidation through AuthBroker, so there is no two-writer race by construction (human: ~4 hr / CC: ~20 min)
✅ Tests construct a fresh in-memory adapter per case; no cross-test leakage and the concurrency claim is testable with an interleaving test
❌ SessionMint gains a dependency on AuthBroker (or a narrow invalidation interface) rather than on the cache directly

options.label: 1B) Inject, keep two writers
options.description:
✅ Constructor injection fixes test isolation and hidden coupling with the same cheap change (human: ~2 hr / CC: ~10 min)
✅ Neither service needs to know about the other; both depend only on the AuthCache interface
❌ The unserialized two-writer race on a shared tenant key stays; you must document key-scoped idempotency and still cannot prove ordering

options.label: 1C) Keep module-level global
options.description:
✅ Zero plan changes and no constructor churn (human: 0 / CC: 0)
✅ Matches whatever the current codebase already does for other shared modules
❌ Test isolation, hidden coupling, and the write race all stay; a revoked token surviving in cache is a silent cross-tenant failure

questions.question:
D7 — Issue 3 [P1] (confidence 8/10) PLAN.md:23-24 — validateAndDispatch() is 60 lines with three nested try/catch blocks and each catch swallows a different error class. How should error handling be restructured?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, Section 2 Code Quality.
ELI10: Three nested try/catch blocks that each swallow an error mean a failed token check, a failed policy lookup, or a failed dispatch can all turn into 'nothing happened'. In auth, a swallowed error is the worst outcome: the user either gets silently denied with no reason or, worse, falls through to a code path that treats missing data as valid. Splitting the function into three named steps with one error boundary that maps each error class to an explicit outcome (deny with reason, retry, or rethrow) makes every failure visible and every branch testable.
Stakes if we pick wrong: A swallowed IDP error on a revocation check can let a revoked session through; a swallowed policy error can deny a whole tenant with no log line to debug from.
Recommendation: A because swallowing is never acceptable in an auth path, and three small pure functions plus one boundary is both DRY and explicit. Each error class then has exactly one place where its handling is decided.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=2/10
Net: three 15-line functions with one visible error map versus one 60-line function that can fail silently three different ways.

options.label: 3A) Decompose + single error boundary (recommended)
options.description:
✅ Split into validateToken, resolvePolicy, dispatch; one outer boundary maps TokenError, PolicyError, DispatchError to explicit deny/retry/rethrow with a log line and metric each (human: ~4 hr / CC: ~20 min)
✅ Each step is unit-testable alone and the error map is one table-driven test; no error class can be silently dropped
❌ Touches the dispatch entry point that the per-tenant flag from Issue 2 also lives in, so sequence this refactor first

options.label: 3B) Keep shape, log in each catch
options.description:
✅ Minimal diff; add a structured log and metric inside each existing catch (human: ~1 hr / CC: ~5 min)
✅ Failures become visible in logs without changing control flow
❌ Still three nested blocks in one 60-line function; swallow-then-continue semantics remain and are still hard to test per branch

options.label: 3C) Leave as-is
options.description:
✅ No change to a function that presumably works today (human: 0 / CC: 0)
✅ No risk of altering control flow in the dispatch path
❌ Three silent failure modes in the auth path persist and the new AuthBroker path inherits them

questions.question:
D9 — Issue 5 [P2] (confidence 8/10) PLAN.md:31-32 — Token validation makes 5 sequential IDP calls; the plan says 'Promise.all trivially'. How should the parallelization be done?
Project/branch/task: main, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, Section 4 Performance.
ELI10: Five calls in a row means login latency is the sum of five network round trips. Running them at once cuts that to the slowest single call. But 'just wrap in Promise.all' is not the whole story: Promise.all rejects on the first failure and leaves the other four requests running in the background, and none of the calls has a timeout today. For auth, fail-fast is correct (all five checks must pass), so Promise.all is the right primitive, but each call needs a timeout and the losers need to be cancelled so a slow IDP does not pile up open connections under load.
Stakes if we pick wrong: Bare Promise.all with no timeout means one hung IDP endpoint hangs every login indefinitely; allSettled would let a login proceed with a failed check unless you add aggregation logic that fail-fast already gives you.
Recommendation: A because all five checks are required for a valid token, so fail-fast semantics match the domain, and adding an AbortController plus per-call timeout is a few lines that turns a latency win into a resilience win too.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=6/10
Net: parallel with cancellation and timeouts versus parallel with dangling requests and no upper bound on login time.

options.label: 5A) Promise.all + shared AbortController + per-call timeout (recommended)
options.description:
✅ All five run in parallel, first failure aborts the rest, every call bounded by a timeout mapped to TokenError for the Issue 3 error boundary (human: ~3 hr / CC: ~15 min)
✅ Login latency drops from sum-of-five to max-of-one and a hung IDP degrades to a clear timeout instead of a hang
❌ Requires the IDP client to accept an abort signal; if it does not, wrap it once in a small adapter

options.label: 5B) Bare Promise.all as planned
options.description:
✅ One-line change that gets the full latency win (human: ~30 min / CC: ~2 min)
✅ Fail-fast semantics already match 'all checks must pass'
❌ No timeout and no cancellation: a slow IDP hangs login and losing requests keep running after the first rejection

options.label: 5C) Promise.allSettled + aggregate
options.description:
✅ Every call completes so you get a full picture of which checks failed for diagnostics (human: ~2 hr / CC: ~10 min)
✅ No dangling requests since all settle before you proceed
❌ Login waits for the slowest call even when the first one already failed; you re-implement fail-fast by hand in the aggregation

questions.question:
D4 — Complexity check triggered: 4 new classes across 12 files. Reduce scope or proceed as-is?
Project/branch/task: main branch, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, Step 0 scope gate.
ELI10: The plan adds four new classes (TokenStore, SessionMint, AuthCache, RequestPolicy) plus AuthBroker, touching 12 files (PLAN.md:35-36). The existing cache adapter already stores tokens keyed by tenant, evicts, and invalidates (PLAN.md:7-13), so TokenStore looks like a second token store next to the first. RequestPolicy has no stated behavior beyond a policy decision, which is usually typed config plus one pure function, not a class. Every extra class is a second place a 3am on-call engineer has to look when a tenant's token is stale.
Stakes if we pick wrong: over-build means two token stores that can disagree on validity; under-build means we cut a class that had a real reason to exist that the plan did not state.
Recommendation: A because the adapter already owns token storage and the plan gives TokenStore and RequestPolicy no responsibility that justifies a class; AuthBroker, SessionMint, and AuthCache-as-injected-seam carry the actual goal.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: fewer moving parts and one source of truth for tokens vs keeping the plan's original decomposition.

options.label: Reduce: cut TokenStore + RequestPolicy class (recommended)
options.description: (human: ~1 day less / CC: ~10 min less) ✅ One token store: the existing adapter behind AuthCache; no second cache that can disagree on validity. ✅ RequestPolicy becomes a typed config object plus a pure evaluate() function, trivially unit-testable. ✅ Drops to 2-3 new classes and roughly 8-9 files. ❌ If TokenStore held state the adapter cannot (e.g. refresh-token secrets), that need must be re-stated and re-planned.

options.label: Proceed as-is with 4 classes
options.description: (human: ~3 days / CC: ~45 min) ✅ Keeps whatever unstated reasons the author had for each class. ✅ No re-planning before the review continues. ❌ Two token-holding components (adapter + TokenStore) and a class for what is likely config; more surface for the tests and the on-call engineer.

options.label: Reduce further: also drop AuthCache facade
options.description: (human: ~1.5 days less / CC: ~15 min less) ✅ Services inject the existing adapter directly; smallest possible diff, one fewer indirection. ✅ Existing adapter tests already cover the store the services talk to. ❌ Loses the seam where tenant-scoped or service-facing helpers would live; if the adapter API is wide, both services re-implement the same wrapping (DRY hit).

questions.question:
D5 — Issue 1: AuthBroker and SessionMint both mutate a module-level global AuthCache with no serialization. How should the cache be owned?
Project/branch/task: main branch, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, Architecture review.
ELI10: Both new services import the same cache object from a module and write to it (PLAN.md:19-20), and the plan says nothing serializes those writes (PLAN.md:10). Two writers on one shared object is how a token minted for tenant A lands under tenant B's key, or a revocation gets overwritten by a stale mint a few milliseconds later. A module-level global also means tests share state across files and you cannot swap in a fake without hacking the module cache.
Stakes if we pick wrong: cross-tenant token leakage or a revoked session staying valid, which in auth is a security incident, not a bug.
Recommendation: 1A because a single writer plus constructor injection removes the race by design instead of by lock, matches your explicit-over-clever and well-tested preferences, and costs minutes with CC.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=2/10
Net: eliminate the race structurally vs paper over it with a lock vs accept a latent auth race.

options.label: 1A: Inject AuthCache; AuthBroker sole writer (recommended)
options.description: (human: ~1 day / CC: ~15 min) Completeness 10/10. ✅ One writer: SessionMint returns a minted session and AuthBroker commits it via one write-through method (putIfAbsent / compare-and-set on tenant key + policy version). ✅ Constructor injection from one composition root makes every test a fresh instance with a fake adapter; no module-cache hacks. ✅ Contract test proves two concurrent mints for the same tenant key yield exactly one cache entry. ❌ SessionMint's public shape changes from 'mutate cache' to 'return value', so its callers need the broker in the loop.

options.label: 1B: Keep module export, add per-tenant-key mutex
options.description: (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min) Completeness 7/10. ✅ Smallest change to the plan's current shape; both services keep writing. ✅ Serializes writes per tenant key so revoke-then-mint ordering is preserved. ❌ Lock is a runtime guard, not a design boundary; a third writer added later is one forgotten import away from the same race. ❌ Global still leaks state across tests and hides the dependency.

options.label: 1C: Do nothing, keep as planned
options.description: (human: 0 / CC: 0) Completeness 2/10. ✅ No change to the plan or its file count. ✅ If the runtime is truly single-threaded and every write is synchronous, the race window may be tiny. ❌ 'Tiny' is not 'zero' across await points in token validation, and the plan already says mutations are not serialized.

questions.question:
D7 — Issue 3: validateAndDispatch() nests three try/catch blocks that each swallow an error class. How should it be restructured?
Project/branch/task: main branch, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, Code quality review.
ELI10: One 60-line function does validation and dispatch with three nested try/catch blocks, and each catch swallows a different error class (PLAN.md:23-24). Swallowing means the function keeps going as if nothing failed. In an auth path that can mean a token that failed a check still gets dispatched, and the only trace is a log line nobody reads. Splitting it into small stages with one explicit result type makes every failure visible, typed, and testable.
Stakes if we pick wrong: silent auth failures that look like success from the outside, and a function nobody wants to touch.
Recommendation: 3A because explicit typed outcomes beat clever catch-and-continue, each stage becomes a pure unit with its own tests, and it is a 15-minute job with CC.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=6/10, C=2/10
Net: explicit failure surface and testable stages vs a smaller edit that keeps the swallowing shape.

options.label: 3A: Split into stages, one typed error boundary (recommended)
options.description: (human: ~half day / CC: ~15 min) Completeness 10/10. ✅ validateToken(), resolvePolicy(), dispatch() as separate functions, each returning a typed Result (ok | AuthError subtype) instead of throwing into a swallowing catch. ✅ One boundary at the top maps every AuthError to an explicit response or rethrow with tenant context; nothing is swallowed. ✅ Each stage gets a test per success and per error class; 3 error classes = at least 3 negative tests. ❌ More small functions and a Result type; slightly larger diff than an in-place patch.

options.label: 3B: Keep one function, stop swallowing
options.description: (human: ~1 hour / CC: ~5 min) Completeness 6/10. ✅ Minimal diff: each catch rethrows a typed AuthError with context instead of swallowing. ✅ No new types or file moves. ❌ Still 60 lines with three nesting levels; hard to test each branch in isolation. ❌ The next person adding a fourth check will add a fourth nested try/catch.

options.label: 3C: Leave as-is
options.description: (human: 0 / CC: 0) Completeness 2/10. ✅ Zero risk of breaking whatever the swallowing currently hides. ✅ No effort. ❌ Auth failures stay silent; the plan itself calls this out as a smell and the refactor is the natural moment to fix it.

questions.question:
D9 — Issue 5: Token validation makes 5 sequential IDP calls. How should they be parallelized, and what happens when one fails?
Project/branch/task: main branch, PLAN.md Multi-tenant Auth Refactor, Performance review.
ELI10: Every login waits for five identity-provider round trips one after another (PLAN.md:31-32). Running them at once cuts that wait to roughly the slowest single call. The catch is failure semantics: Promise.all rejects on the first failure but leaves the other four requests running, and you need to decide whether a partial result is ever usable for validation. For auth it is not: every check must pass, so fail-fast is correct, but the in-flight calls should be cancelled and the failure typed so it lands in the Issue 3 error boundary instead of a swallowed catch.
Stakes if we pick wrong: either users wait 5x longer than needed, or a partial failure produces a confusing aggregate error and orphaned requests hammer the IDP during an outage.
Recommendation: 5A because validation needs all five results, fail-fast is the right semantics, and adding an AbortController plus one shared timeout is a few lines that also protect the IDP when it is degraded.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=8/10, C=1/10
Net: fast, bounded, cancellable validation vs bare Promise.all vs the current 5x latency.

options.label: 5A: Promise.all + AbortController + shared timeout, typed failure (recommended)
options.description: (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min) Completeness 10/10. ✅ Latency drops from sum-of-five to max-of-one on the login hot path. ✅ First failure aborts the other four via one AbortSignal and surfaces as a typed IdpValidationError with which check failed, feeding the Issue 3 boundary. ✅ Tests: all succeed, one rejects (others aborted), one times out, IDP 5xx. ❌ Slightly more code than a one-line Promise.all; needs the IDP client to accept an AbortSignal.

options.label: 5B: Bare Promise.all
options.description: (human: ~30 min / CC: ~3 min) Completeness 8/10. ✅ Same latency win with a one-line change. ✅ Fail-fast semantics match 'all checks must pass'. ❌ Remaining four requests keep running after the first rejection; during an IDP incident that multiplies load on a struggling dependency. ❌ No shared deadline, so one hung call hangs the login.

options.label: 5C: Leave sequential
options.description: (human: 0 / CC: 0) Completeness 1/10. ✅ Simplest possible control flow and error attribution. ✅ Lowest instantaneous load on the IDP. ❌ Users pay five round trips on every login; the plan itself calls the calls independent.

answers.D9 \u2014 Issue 5: Token validation make: 5A: Promise.all + AbortController + shared timeout, typed failure (recommended)
